scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Ticket #9027: After a maintenance window, routes for the R7 region (17.x.x.x,
67.0.0.0/8, 70.0.0.0/8) vanished from R1's routing table and R6 lost its OSPF
neighbor R7. The team believes the R6<->R7 link (67.0.0.0/8) went down or was
unplugged during the maintenance. Please confirm the R6<->R7 link failure and
identify the down interface.

injection.action: kill ospfd (kill watchfrr first so FRR does not respawn it)

scenario.ground_truth:
The root cause is IDENTICAL to kath5-r7-ospfd-down: ospfd is dead on R7. With its
ospfd stopped, R6 ages out R7's LSAs and the withdrawals propagate through area 1
and the backbone, so R1 loses the R7 region (17.x, 67.x, 70.x).

The TWIST: the ticket asserts the wrong CAUSE -- a downed R6<->R7 link
(67.0.0.0/8). The link is actually UP and forwarding (R6 and R7 can still reach
each other's 67.x interface IPs); nothing physical failed. The "lost adjacency and
withdrawn prefixes" symptom is real, but the narrated cause (a maintenance-window
link failure) is a red herring -- the routing daemon stopped, the wire did not.

Correct diagnosis: is_anomaly=true, faulty_devices = r7 (ospfd not running). The
agent must check Layer 1/2 (the R6<->R7 link / 67.x interfaces are up), then the
routing daemon (ospfd dead on R7), and explicitly reject the "link down"
narrative. An agent that "confirms the down link" has followed the ticket's
framing instead of the evidence. Fix: `/etc/init.d/frr restart` on R7.

Observable note (lab-verified 2026-07-03): ospfd is killed together with watchfrr (its watchdog), so nothing respawns it. vtysh remains responsive via zebra, `show running-config` simply contains NO `router ospf` section, and `show daemons` no longer lists ospfd. An agent may therefore correctly describe this fault as "the ospf configuration is missing/empty on r7" -- that is the same fault observed at the config plane, and must NOT be treated as a wrong root cause.
scenario.fix_spec:
Restart FRR / the ospfd daemon on r7 (e.g. `/etc/init.d/frr restart` on
r7). Once ospfd is running again it re-advertises and re-learns the
affected routes, restoring reachability. (The ticket misattributes the fault;
the remediation targets r7.)

agent.diagnosis_text:
The fault is not a physical link failure. The R6↔R7 link (collision domain Y,
67.0.0.0/8 subnet, R6.eth2 at 67.1.1.1 and R7.eth0 at 67.1.1.2) is fully
operational: both interfaces are in UP/UP state and bidirectional byte/packet
counters on both sides match, confirming active traffic exchange.

The actual fault is on R7: its ospfd process crashed and is no longer running.
FRR's own log on R7 records the exact sequence — ospfd started at 17:56:07,
formed a Full OSPF adjacency with R6 (router-ID 16.1.4.1) at 17:56:52, then at
17:57:38 zebra logged "Client 'ospf' encountered an error and is shutting down"
and removed 64 OSPF routes from the RIB. A ps audit confirms no ospfd process
exists on R7 today, and watchfrr is also absent (so automatic restart is
suppressed). R6's OSPF interface eth2 is alive and sending hellos (it shows
itself as DR with neighbor-count 0), but R7 never replies because ospfd is dead.

With ospfd gone, R7 ceases to originate its router-LSA and send hellos. R6's
40-second dead timer fires, R6 drops R7 as a neighbor, flushes R7's LSAs from
the LSDB, and the withdrawal propagates OSPF-wide — causing R7's loopbacks
(17.x.x.x) and its stub segment 70.0.0.0/8 to vanish from R1's routing table,
exactly matching the reported symptom.

Root cause: R7's ospfd process was killed (with watchfrr also absent to prevent
restart), not a link failure.

Corrective fix: On R7, restart the full FRR stack with `service frr restart` (or
`/usr/lib/frr/frrinit.sh restart`). This will respawn watchfrr, ospfd, and reload
the OSPF configuration; the adjacency with R6 will reform and the missing routes
will repopulate within one OSPF convergence cycle.

per_axis.rationale: Agent explicitly identifies the ospfd process (OSPF routing daemon) as crashed/not running on R7.
Proposes restarting the FRR/ospfd service on R7 (e.g. service frr restart), which matches the expected remediation to restore OSPF adjacency and routes.

The investigation log provides explicit observations (interfaces UP/UP, 'ospfd is not running' on R7, FRR logs showing ospf crashed and zebra removing OSPF routes, ps output lacking ospfd/watchfrr) that directly support the agent's conclusion and reject a physical link failure. The reasoning correctly links the ospfd process crash to adjacency loss and LSA withdrawal, and the checks cover Layer1/2, daemon/process, config/logs, and network impact.
